Introduction
Imaging studies are essential for a comprehensive evaluation of the knee joint.
Radiographic findings should correlate with a patient’s history and physical examination
to obtain an accurate diagnosis. Plain radiography often is the initial imaging modality;
however, additional imaging studies, including CT, MRI, ultrasonography, and nuclear
medicine scanning, may be required to provide additional information to assist in the
diagnosis and management of knee pathology. Finally, radiographic evaluation is
necessary during the postoperative period to monitor for complications and determine
the etiology of postoperative pain.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Plain radiography
Orthogonal view—Imaging studies should include at least two perpendicular views: AP
(Figure 1) and lateral (Figure 2; Resource 1)


Radiography
Plain radiography is the initial imaging modality for evaluation of the knee. Orthogonal
views, including AP and lateral radiographs, are necessary to understand the three-
dimensional relationship of imaging findings. An AP radiograph assesses the coronal
plane and is obtained with the knee in full extension. A weight-bearing view is preferred
to accurately assess the joint under mechanical load and as it is more sensitive in
detecting degenerative joint disease1 (Resource 2). The lateral radiograph evaluates the
sagittal plane and is obtained with the knee in approximately 30° of flexion. Overlapping
femoral condyles should be observed for ideal image rotation and quality. The lateral
radiograph may aid in evaluating patellar height, tibial slope, and subluxation of the joint
secondary to injury to the cruciate ligaments. Images can be obtained with the use of a
calibrated reference marker to aid in the preoperative templating of components before
total knee arthroplasty (TKA)2 (Resource 3).
Additional radiographic views can be obtained to evaluate for pathology not well-
visualized on standard AP or lateral views. For instance, the PA flexion view is a weight-
bearing radiograph obtained with the knee in approximately 30° to 45° of flexion. The
view allows for better assessment of the posterior aspect of the femoral condyles as
they articulate with the tibial plateau and may improve the detection of osteoarthritis3
(Resource 4). Similarly, an intercondylar notch view is obtained with the knee in 40° of
flexion and is used to evaluate the intercondylar notch of the distal femur for loose
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:58 PM
AAOS | Radiographic Evaluation of the Knee
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000017
8/30

bodies, notch width, and osteophyte formation. Evaluation of the patellofemoral
compartment is critical; it is assessed via tangential views of the patellofemoral joint. A
Merchant view can be obtained to evaluate the patellofemoral joint with the knee in 45°
of flexion and the x-ray beam directed caudally. This view is helpful in assessing the joint
space, alignment, tracking, and morphology of the patellofemoral joint. Oblique
radiographs can be obtained to evaluate for subtle fractures involving the articular
surface. A full-length mechanical axis radiograph allows for visualization of mechanical
and anatomic alignment of the entire lower extremity, which aids in preoperative
surgical planning (Resource 5) and in the postoperative evaluation of joint alignment4,5
(Resource 6).
Clinical indications
Trauma—Non–weight-bearing radiographs may help identify acute injury without the risk of
fracture displacement.
Fracture of the distal femur, proximal tibia, proximal fibula, patella, or tibial tuberosity
Dislocation or subluxation of the tibiofemoral or patellofemoral joint
Pathognomonic avulsion injuries may indicate ligament injury, which cannot be explicitly
observed on plain radiography.
Knee pain
Osteoarthritis—Radiography may identify subchondral sclerosis, joint space narrowing,
subchondral cysts, osteophytes, and joint subluxation (Figure 6).
matory arthropathy—Symmetric loss of joint space, peripheral bone erosions
Patellofemoral disease—Malalignment, osteophytes, cysts, loss of joint space
Other etiologies—Osteochondritis dissecans, osteonecrosis, neoplasm, infection
Postoperative complications—Routine monitoring of patients who undergo TKA may detect
complications, such as component loosening, malalignment, polyethylene wear, osteolysis.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:58 PM
AAOS | Radiographic Evaluation of the Knee
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000017
9/30

Figure 6 Weight-bearing AP radiograph of bilateral knees demonstrates right knee osteoarthritis
with joint space narrowing, osteophyte formation, subchondral sclerosis, and a small
subchondral cyst in the medial distal femur. (Image courtesy of Edward S. Hur, MD, Chicago, IL.)

Clinical Indications
Plain radiographs of the knee in patients with trauma should be obtained as non–weight-
bearing images to assess for acute injury, limiting the risk of fracture displacement
associated with weight bearing. A systematic review of the distal femur, proximal tibia,
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:58 PM
AAOS | Radiographic Evaluation of the Knee
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000017
10/30

proximal fibula, and patella should be performed. Any cortical irregularity, linear lucency,
or dislocation should be noted. Intra-articular effusion or lipohemarthrosis can be
visualized on the lateral radiograph and often is a sign of intra-articular injury. Trauma
also may result in ligamentous injury, which is poorly observed on plain radiographs;
however, pathognomonic osseous findings of ligament injury can be observed. For
example, a Segond fracture is a small avulsion fracture from the anterolateral tibial
plateau and is strongly associated with anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury6 (Resource
7).
Osteoarthritis is characterized by a combination of joint space narrowing, osteophyte
formation, subchondral sclerosis, and subchondral cysts. Depending on associated
injuries and the degree of degeneration, subluxation and malalignment of the joint can
be observed7 (Resource 8).
Joint space narrowing also is observed in patients with inflammatory arthropathy, such
as rheumatoid arthritis (Resource 9); however, inflammatory pathology may be
distinguished from osteoarthritis via peripheral bone erosions and symmetric joint space
loss in the medial and lateral tibiofemoral compartments, which are more characteristic
of inflammatory arthropathy.8 Assessment of the patellofemoral joint via an axial view
may reveal joint space narrowing, indicating cartilage loss secondary to degenerative or
inflammatory arthropathy. In addition, patellofemoral malalignment and instability are
associated with increased patellar shift and lateral tilt of the patella9 (Resource 10).
Knee pain is associated with multiple etiologies. Osteochondritis dissecans of the knee is
a localized osteonecrosis of the subchondral bone and damage of the articular cartilage
commonly observed in adolescent males secondary to chronic repetitive trauma.
Radiographs may reveal a crescent-shaped lucency involving the subchondral bone most
commonly affecting the posterolateral aspect of the medial femoral condyle and is best
observed on intercondylar notch radiographs10 (Resource 11). Spontaneous
osteonecrosis of the knee may produce a similar appearance with subchondral lucency.
Advanced disease may result in collapse of subchondral bone but typically is observed in
older patient populations11 (Resource 12). Surgeons must also evaluate for possible
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:58 PM
AAOS | Radiographic Evaluation of the Knee
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000017
11/30

osteolytic and osteoblastic lesions that may represent a neoplasm such as
osteosarcoma, Ewing sarcoma, or giant cell tumors, which warrant further investigation.
Routine postoperative monitoring of patients who undergo TKA is performed via a series
of standard plain radiographs. Interval radiographic images should be compared to
assess for changes in component positioning and alignment. Component loosening may
be observed as continuous radiolucent lines surrounding the implant, fracture of the
cement mantle or implant, and interval change in component positioning. Serial
radiographs are used to detect the rate of polyethylene liner wear. Osteolytic cysts
should be noted, and radiographs should be compared chronologically to detect
progression. Joint instability may be observed as subluxation of the patellofemoral or
tibiofemoral joint.
Computed Tomography
Definition of CT
CT is a three-dimensional study performed with ionizing radiation that provides enhanced
bone detail.
Clinical indications
Imaging in the axial, sagittal, and coronal planes to help visualize fracture lines, fracture
displacement, or fracture extension to the knee joint
Aids in the evaluation of infectious and neoplastic disease that may involve the osseous
structures of the knee
Three-dimensional CT reconstruction may aid in preoperative planning for complex intra-
articular fractures, multiplanar osteotomy for limb malalignment, and reconstitution of bone
loss in joint arthroplasty.
Postoperative evaluation may aid in the diagnosis of complications, such as nonunion of
fracture fixation, component loosening, or osteolysis after TKA
Axial plane imaging of the lower extremity may aid in assessing the rotational alignment of
the components of a TKA implant in patients with patellar maltracking (Figure 7).
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:58 PM
AAOS | Radiographic Evaluation of the Knee
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000017
12/30

Figure 7 Axial CT scan of a distal femur shows 5° of internal rotation of the femoral component
after total knee arthroplasty. The surgical epicondylar axis connects the lateral epicondyle and
the medial sulcus of the medial epicondyle. The posterior condylar line connects the posterior
condylar surfaces of the implant. (Reproduced with permission from Berger RA, Crossett LS,
Jacobs JJ, Rubash HE: Malrotation causing patellofemoral complications after total knee
arthroplasty. Clin Orthop Relat Res 1998;356:144-153.)

Computed Tomography
Similar to plain radiography, CT involves the use of ionizing radiation to produce cross-
sectional images in multiple planes. The tomographic images produced via CT show
osseous structures with fine detail and eliminate artifact from intervening tissues that
may hinder visualization at the area of interest. In addition, contrast agents can be used
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:58 PM
AAOS | Radiographic Evaluation of the Knee
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000017
13/30

to better differentiate between soft-tissue structures; however, contrast agents often are
not administered in the evaluation of soft tissues12 (Resource 13).
The enhanced detail and cross-sectional images in multiple planes afforded by CT enable
the thorough evaluation of osseous structures. In patients with neoplasia, CT can
determine the extent of osseous involvement and further characterize osseous lesions.
For example, osteoid osteoma, a benign bone tumor that may cause pain around the
knee, is observed as a well-defined central nidus with surrounding reactive sclerosis on
CT. Similarly, infectious processes that involve bone can be further characterized via CT.
A key advantage of CT is the ability to create three-dimensional reconstruction images
that aid in preoperative planning. It may provide accurate measurements of fracture
displacement, the degree of fracture comminution, intra-articular extension of fracture
lines, and fractures involving prosthetic implants. Articular bone defects can be
identified, and volumetric analysis can be performed with CT before reconstruction.
Preoperative CT can be used for computer navigation, patient-specific instrumentation,
and robot-assisted surgery.
Postoperatively, CT can aid in the diagnosis of delayed union and nonunion after
fracture fixation. In arthroplasty, it may allow for further evaluation of osteolytic cysts
surrounding prosthetic components that may result in component subsidence or
loosening. Malalignment or malrotation of TKA implants, which may contribute to joint
instability or patellar maltracking, can be diagnosed and quantified
accurately13 (Resource 14).
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI definition
Three-dimensional imaging modality that uses a strong magnetic field to generate images of
tissue
Increasing the strength of the magnetic field (measured in Tesla units) increases the
resolution of images.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:58 PM
AAOS | Radiographic Evaluation of the Knee
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000017
14/30

An injected intravenous or intra-articular contrast agent may help delineate specific tissues
of interest.
Multiple sequences (T1-weighted, T2-weighted, short tau inversion recovery) are available
and produce different signal intensities of various tissue structures.
Clinical indications
Cruciate ligaments—The presence of edema or intra-articular fluid, disruption of ligament
fibers, and atypical ligament contour may suggest injury to the ACL or the posterior cruciate
ligament (Figure 8).
Patterns of meniscal injury can be identified by location (anterior, mid body, posterior, root),
pattern (horizontal, longitudinal, radial, complex), and displacement (Figures 9 and 10).
Articular cartilage—MRI can identify the degree of articular cartilage injury (chondrosis, full-
thickness cartilage loss) as well as the presence of associated bone marrow edema and its
location (medial condyle, lateral condyle, trochlea, patella).
Extra-articular ligaments—Edema, avulsion, and discontinuity may be identified in the medial
collateral ligament, lateral collateral ligament, and associated posteromedial and
posterolateral ligamentous complexes.
Tendon injury—MRI can be used to assess the continuity of the quadriceps and the patellar
tendon.
Neurovascular structures—MRI can be used to assess the margin of resection for a
neoplasm, identify vascular malformation, and define the location of nerves or vessels
relative to popliteal cysts.
Bone marrow—MRI can be used to evaluate for pathology of bone marrow, including
contusions, stress fractures, osteomyelitis, necrosis, and malignancy.


Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI uses a strong magnetic field and detects differences in tissue signal intensity to
produce an image. Unlike plain radiography or CT, MRI does not involve the use of
ionizing radiation. MRI provides excellent contrast resolution and is useful for the
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:58 PM
AAOS | Radiographic Evaluation of the Knee
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000017
18/30

evaluation of soft-tissue structures, such as muscle, tendon, fat, cartilage, and ligaments.
Intravenous contrast may further delineate tissues of interest to evaluate for specific
pathology. To better assess for joint pathology, contrast agents can be injected intra-
articularly; this technique is known as magnetic resonance arthrography. Increased
magnetic field strength, measured in Tesla units, may improve the resolution of images.
For example, 3.0T MRI is associated with a higher resolution than 1.5T MRI. Multiple
sequences can be generated by changing the imaging parameters, such as magnetic
pulse, which affects the appearance of particular tissues. For example, a T1-weighted
image has specific parameters that cause fluid to appear dark, whereas a T2-weighted
image causes fluid to appear bright14 (Resource 15).
Compared with CT and plain radiography, MRI is superior for the imaging of soft-tissue
structures. Injury to the intra-articular ligaments is well-visualized on MRI. The ACL is the
most commonly injured ligament in the knee, and rupture of the ACL can be diagnosed
on MRI with more than 95% accuracy15 (Resource 16). Such injury is best observed on
T2-weighted sagittal MRIs. Associated contusion of the lateral femoral condyle sulcus
and the posterolateral proximal tibia can be observed as increased signal intensity in the
subchondral bone and bone marrow. Similarly, injury to the posterior cruciate ligament
also can be observed. Extra-articular ligamentous structures also can be injured,
resulting in joint instability. The integrity of the lateral collateral ligament, medial
collateral ligament, posterolateral corner complex, and posteromedial complex can be
evaluated via MRI. In addition, tendinosis of the patellar and quadriceps tendon results
in disorganized fibers and tendon thickening that is evident on MRI. Complete
discontinuity of the tendon can be observed on the MRIs of patients with a tendon
rupture.
MRI is the most accurate imaging modality for the diagnosis of meniscal pathology.
Intrasubstance signal of the meniscus is indicative of a tear and can be characterized by
location (anterior root, anterior horn, body, posterior horn, and posterior root), pattern
(horizontal, longitudinal, radial, complex), and degree of displacement. Associated
parameniscal cysts and meniscal extrusion are secondary signs of meniscal injury. A
bucket-handle meniscus tear results from a displaced vertical tear of the meniscus that
may cause a mechanical block to joint range of motion and is observed as a double
posterior cruciate ligament sign on MRI.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:58 PM
AAOS | Radiographic Evaluation of the Knee
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000017
19/30

A detailed evaluation of the articular cartilage can be performed via MRI and is best
visualized on proton-density or T2-weighted images. Articular cartilage degeneration, as
observed on the MRIs of patients with osteoarthritis, can be graded and characterized as
partial-thickness or full-thickness cartilage loss. Focal cartilage defects also can be
observed on the MRIs of patients with traumatic chondral defects. Preoperatively, MRI
can be used to create patient-specific instrumentation for TKA.
MRI is useful for evaluating neoplastic disease about the knee to better characterize
osseous and soft-tissue masses. If masses are large and require resection, their
relationship to the neurovascular structures coursing across the knee joint should be
noted. Identification of the proximity of the mass to these neurovascular structures is
critical for surgical planning. In addition to compression of these structures by masses,
compression by other structures and the formation of vascular malformations can be
identified via MRI.
Ultrasonography
Definition of ultrasonography
Uses a transducer to produce high-frequency sound waves that are reflected by tissue to
create an image
No ionizing radiation is used.
Noninvasive
Indications
Evaluation of soft-tissue structures, such as tendons, ligaments, and soft-tissue masses
(Figure 11)
Evaluation of vascular structures for peripheral vascular disease, pseudoaneurysms, and
deep vein thrombosis
Dynamic assessment of tissue
Can aid in performing procedures, such as aspiration or injection
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:58 PM
AAOS | Radiographic Evaluation of the Knee
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000017
20/30

Figure 11 Longitudinal ultrasonographic image shows a complete quadriceps tendon tear. A
hypoechoic defect (arrow) is observed between the outlined proximal and distal stumps of the
quadriceps tendon (QT). (Reproduced with permission from Alves TI, Girish G, Kalume Brigido M,
Jacobson JA: US of the knee: Scanning techniques, pitfalls, and pathologic conditions.
Radiographics 2016;36[6]:1759-1775.)

Ultrasonography
Ultrasonography involves the use of a transducer to produce high-frequency sound
waves that are reflected by tissue. The reflected sound waves are used to produce an
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:58 PM
AAOS | Radiographic Evaluation of the Knee
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000017
21/30

image. No ionizing radiation is used for ultrasonography. In addition, doppler
ultrasonography can be used to assess the flow of fluid16 (Resource 17).
While MRI typically is the imaging modality of choice for detailed visualization of most
soft-tissue pathology, especially intra-articular pathology, ultrasonography can also be
used for the evaluation of soft-tissue structures of the knee. Fluid collections, such as a
joint effusion or a Baker cyst, can be identified. Tendons, including the patellar or
quadriceps tendons, can be assessed, and findings—including tendinosis, partial tears,
or complete ruptures—may be identified. A dynamic assessment of tissue can be
performed, which may aid in differentiating partial tears from complete tears of the
quadriceps or patellar tendon if the physical examination is equivocal. Additional
structures that can be evaluated using ultrasonography include the pes anserine bursa,
prepatellar bursa, medial collateral ligament, and lateral collateral ligament. Doppler
ultrasonography is an imaging modality that measures the flow of fluid and can be
useful in detecting increased vascularity of inflamed tissues and pathology of large blood
vessels in patients with peripheral vascular disease, pseudoaneurysm, and deep vein
thrombosis. In addition, arthrofibrosis after TKA may be identified, with the detection of
synovial membrane thickening and neovascularity.17 Finally, ultrasonography can ensure
proper needle placement during procedures such as aspiration and injection.18
Nuclear Medicine
Definition of nuclear medicine
Uses a radiopharmaceutical tracer injection that serves as a marker for biologic activity by
capturing the amount of emitted radiation.
Multiple radiotracers have been used to measure various biologic activity, including
technetium Tc-99, gallium Ga-67, Indium In-111, and F-18 fluorodeoxyglucose.
Various modalities of scintigraphy are available, including bone scintigraphy, positron
emission tomography, single photon emission computed tomography, and leukocyte
scanning.
Provides a nonspecific study that does not define the etiology of an abnormality but rather
the presence of an abnormality, which may correlate with a clinical concern.
Clinical indications
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:58 PM
AAOS | Radiographic Evaluation of the Knee
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000017
22/30

Nuclear medicine often is used to aid in the diagnosis of neoplasia, infection, occult fracture,
bone healing, the active phases of heterotopic ossification, implant loosening, and failure of
osseointegration as a result of the increased metabolic activity associated with such
pathology.
Nuclear medicine can be used to aid in the diagnosis of periprosthetic joint infections and
component loosening after TKA (Figures 12 and 13).
Increased radionuclide activity in bone may be a normal postoperative finding for as long as
6 to 12 months after fracture repair or arthroplasty.
Figure 12 Radionuclide bone scan of bilateral knees shows increased activity around the femoral,
tibial, and patellar components of a left total knee arthroplasty implant. (Reproduced from
Keeney JA: Radiographic evaluation and surgical anatomy of the knee, in Lieberman JR, ed: AAOS
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:58 PM
AAOS | Radiographic Evaluation of the Knee
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000017
23/30

Comprehensive Orthopaedic Review, ed 3. Rosemont, IL American Academy of Orthopaedic
Surgeons, 2020, pp 470-480.)
Figure 13 Single photon emission CT scan of a knee obtained after unicompartmental knee
arthroplasty shows increased signal intensity surrounding the tibial component, which is
concerning for aseptic loosening. (Reproduced with permission from van der Bruggen W,
Hirschmann MT, Strobel K, et al: SPECT/CT in the postoperative painful knee. Semin Nucl Med
2018;48[5]:439-453.)

Nuclear Medicine
Nuclear medicine imaging studies use a radionuclide injection to assess for biologic
activity. Radiation emissions from the injection are captured and appear bright on
imaging studies, representing greater concentration of the radioisotope-labeled drug.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:58 PM
AAOS | Radiographic Evaluation of the Knee
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000017
24/30

Various imaging techniques and radionuclide injections are available to better serve
various indications.
Bone scintigraphy, also known as bone scanning, is a planar imaging method that
identifies areas of increased osteoblastic activity. It typically involves the use of
technetium Tc-99, which has an affinity for metabolically active bone. Positron emission
tomography (PET) measures cellular activity and typically is performed with positron
emitting radioisotope tracers, such as F-18 fluorodeoxyglucose, which is absorbed into
cells in a manner similar to that of glucose. Leukocyte scanning is used to identify areas
of infection or inflammation by detecting high leukocyte concentration and activity,
typically with Indium In-111 radioactive tracers. Gallium Ga-67 also accumulates in areas
of infection and inflammation; however, it is more time consuming to perform, less
specific, and results in a poorer photon yield compared with leukocyte scanning with the
use of Indium In-111. Single photon emission computed tomography uses the
technology of nuclear medicine to measure biologic activity and produces the same
anatomic detail as that provided by CT to improve the resolution of images and the
localization of the detected biologic activity. While nuclear medicine imaging is useful to
aid in the diagnosis of musculoskeletal pathology, it is important to note that increased
uptake of particular modalities does not define the etiology of symptoms and that
findings must be correlated with overall clinical presentation19,20 (Resources 18 and 19).
The main advantage of nuclear medicine using radionuclide tracers is the ability to
detect metabolic activity. Nuclear medicine may facilitate the work up of neoplastic
conditions, including primary bone tumors and metastatic bone disease. In addition,
infectious processes, such as osteomyelitis, can be identified via various radionuclide
markers, including Indium In-111, gallium Ga-67, or technetium Tc-99. Occult fractures
not observed on plain radiographs may be diagnosed based on the increased activity of
bone at the fracture site. Similarly, early heterotopic ossification that is not observed on
plain radiographs may be detected via nuclear medicine, and the metabolic activity of
heterotopic ossification can be tracked to determine potential management.21
In general, postoperative nuclear medicine is not diagnostic and must be correlated with
a patient’s clinical presentation. Surgeons must consider the timing of imaging because
increased signal uptake may be normal for as long as 6 to 12 months after surgical
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:58 PM
AAOS | Radiographic Evaluation of the Knee
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000017
25/30

treatment. Nuclear medicine can be used for the work up of patients with postoperative
knee pain, including the diagnosis of nonunion in patients with persistent pain after
fracture fixation. The use of nuclear medicine after TKA is associated with decreased
metal artifact compared to MRI or CT and can been used to aid in the diagnosis of
periprosthetic joint infection after TKA with varying sensitivity and specificity.22 In
addition, Single photon emission computed tomography can be used to aid in the
diagnosis of aseptic loosening after TKA23,24 (Resource 20 ).
